title: Chest pain in a 58-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in a suburban clinic in Brisbane. Your next patient is Mr Greg Holloway, a 58-year-old man who has booked a same-day appointment because of chest pain over the past two weeks. He walked in from the car park and is currently comfortable. His observations taken by the practice nurse are: BP 152/94 mmHg, HR 88 regular, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 C.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a focused history from Mr Holloway
- Explain your most likely diagnosis to him
- Outline your immediate management plan
tasks: Take a focused history of the chest pain and cardiovascular risk factors
Explain the most likely diagnosis
Outline the immediate management plan

patient.name: Greg Holloway
patient.persona: Laconic, self-employed tradie who downplays symptoms ('probably just a bit of indigestion, mate'). Speaks in short sentences, mildly irritated at taking time off. Answers what he is asked but does not volunteer details. Becomes quieter and more worried if the doctor mentions the heart, because his father died of a heart attack. Only mentions this morning's episode at rest if asked directly about the most recent episode or whether pain ever comes on at rest.
patient.openingLine: G'day Doc. The wife made me come in. I've been getting this tightness in my chest, reckon it's just indigestion but she won't let it go.
patient.script:
HPI: Two weeks of central chest tightness, 'like a heavy weight', coming on when carrying gear up stairs or walking up the hill to the job site. Radiates to the left shoulder and jaw. Lasts 3-5 minutes and eases with rest. Severity 6/10. Initially only with heavy exertion; over the past four days it has come on with less effort (walking from the ute to the house). HIDDEN CUE 1: This morning at 6 am he had a 15-minute episode while sitting on the edge of the bed tying his boots, with sweating and nausea; it settled on its own. He is pain free now. Associated: mild breathlessness with the pain. Negatives: no palpitations, no syncope, no pleuritic or positional pain, no cough, fever, calf pain, recent travel or reflux symptoms, no pain with swallowing.

PMH: Hypertension diagnosed 5 years ago, 'stopped the tablets a year ago because I felt fine'. Told cholesterol 'a bit high' 3 years ago, never treated. No diabetes known (never checked recently). No previous cardiac history.

Meds: Nil current (previously perindopril 5 mg). Occasional ibuprofen for back pain. No PDE-5 inhibitors. Allergies: nil known.

Family history: Father died of a heart attack aged 61. Brother had stents at 55.

Social: Self-employed plumber. Smokes 20 cigarettes a day for 35 years. Drinks 4-5 full-strength beers most nights, more on weekends. Married, two adult children, lives in a two-storey house. Drives a ute for work. HIDDEN CUE 2: He drove himself here and plans to drive to a job straight after, and has a big job lifting hot water systems this afternoon.

Ideas: Thinks it is indigestion or a pulled muscle. Concerns: Worried (only if asked with empathy) that it is 'the same thing that got Dad'; also worried about losing income. Expectations: Wants some antacids and to get back to work.

If told he needs to go to hospital he initially resists ('Can't I just get a test next week?') but agrees if the doctor explains the risk clearly and kindly.

markingCriteria: Introduces self, confirms identity, establishes rapport and checks current comfort (pain free now) early
Characterises the pain systematically: site, onset, character, radiation, timing, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity
Identifies the crescendo pattern and specifically elicits the episode of pain at rest this morning
Asks about associated features and relevant negatives to exclude differentials (PE, aortic dissection, pericarditis, GORD, musculoskeletal)
Takes a complete cardiovascular risk factor history: smoking, hypertension and non-adherence, lipids, diabetes, family history of premature CAD, alcohol
Takes a medication and allergy history, including stopped antihypertensives and NSAID use
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations, including the fear related to his father's death
States unstable angina / NSTE-ACS as the most likely diagnosis and explains it in plain language
Recommends immediate transfer to ED by ambulance (not driving himself), with an ECG in the clinic while waiting, as per NHFA/CSANZ ACS guidelines
Offers aspirin 300 mg chewed if no contraindication and advises GTN for recurrent pain; tells him to call 000 if pain recurs
Addresses safety: must not drive or do heavy work today; involves wife with permission
Mentions longer term plan in outline: troponin, risk stratification, possible angiography, smoking cessation and risk factor control
expectedDiagnosis: Unstable angina / suspected non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (crescendo angina with rest pain)
teachingPoints: Crescendo angina or any rest pain within the last 24-48 hours is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise: it needs ED assessment, not an outpatient stress test.
In Australian general practice the correct action is a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, aspirin 300 mg, and ambulance transfer via 000; never let the patient drive.
A normal ECG and being pain free now do not exclude NSTE-ACS; serial high-sensitivity troponin in ED is required (NHFA/CSANZ 2016 ACS guideline).
Always ask about the most recent episode and rest pain specifically: patients rarely volunteer it.

Stopped antihypertensives, heavy smoking and a first-degree relative with premature CAD markedly raise pre-test probability; address these once the acute issue is managed (Australian CVD risk guideline 2023).
Explore the patient's fear: a relative's cardiac death is a common hidden concern and drives both denial and later adherence.

title: Breathlessness and ankle swelling in a 74-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are a hospital medical officer (HMO) in the emergency department of a rural hospital in Dubbo, NSW. Mr Frank Petersen, a 74-year-old retired farmer, has presented with three weeks of worsening shortness of breath and swollen ankles. The registrar has taken a history and asked you to examine him. Observations: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 112 irregularly irregular, RR 22, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.6 C.

Your tasks are to:
- Perform a focused cardiovascular and respiratory examination, explaining what you are doing to the patient; the examiner will give you findings
- Tell the examiner your findings and most likely diagnosis
- Outline your initial investigations and management
tasks: Perform a focused cardiovascular and respiratory examination
Present findings and the most likely diagnosis to the examiner
Outline initial investigations and management

patient.name: Frank Petersen
patient.persona: Polite, stoic older man, a bit breathless when speaking in long sentences. Uses plain country language ('I've been puffing like an old steam train'). Cooperative with examination, mildly anxious. Will only mention that he sleeps propped up in the recliner if asked about sleeping. Worries about his wife, who has dementia and depends on him.
patient.openingLine: Morning, Doctor. Sorry to be a nuisance, I just can't get my breath like I used to and my ankles have blown up like balloons.
patient.script:
HPI: Three weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea; now breathless walking 20 metres to the letterbox (previously walked the dog 2 km daily). Orthopnoea: sleeps propped on three pillows, for the last week in the recliner. Wakes at night gasping about twice a week (PND). Bilateral ankle swelling rising to mid-shin. Weight up about 4 kg in three weeks. Palpitations, 'heart fluttering', on and off for a month. Mild dry cough at night. Negatives: no chest pain, no haemoptysis, no fever, no calf pain, no syncope.

PMH: Hypertension for 15 years. Type 2 diabetes (diet and metformin). Myocardial infarction 8 years ago with a stent to LAD. Osteoarthritis of both knees.

Meds: Metformin 1 g BD, ramipril 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Recently started buying over-the-counter naproxen for his knees (HIDDEN CUE 1: only revealed if asked about pain relief or over-the-counter medicines). Allergies: nil.

Family: Nil relevant.

Social: Retired sheep farmer, lives on a property 40 km out of town with wife Joan, who has moderate Alzheimer's dementia; he is her sole carer. HIDDEN CUE 2: If asked about home or who is looking after his wife, becomes worried: 'She's with the neighbour now but she can't be left alone overnight'. Ex-smoker, quit 20 years ago (30 pack-years). Two beers a day. Still drives into town weekly.

Ideas: Thinks it might be 'a chest infection'. Concerns: Who will look after Joan if he is admitted. Expectations: Hopes for tablets and to go home today.
patient.examFindings:
General: Elderly man sitting upright, mildly dyspnoeic at rest, speaking in full sentences. Not cyanosed. No clubbing. Hands warm, no nicotine staining.
Pulse: 112 bpm, irregularly irregular, normal volume. BP 138/86 mmHg.
JVP: Elevated at 6 cm above the sternal angle; positive hepatojugular reflux.
Precordium: Apex beat displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line, diffuse. No heaves or thrills.
Auscultation: S1 variable intensity, S2 normal, S3 not appreciable due to irregular rhythm. Soft 2/6 pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
Chest: Trachea midline. Reduced expansion bilaterally. Stony dull percussion at both bases, right higher than left. Fine bibasal inspiratory crackles to the mid zones. Reduced air entry at the bases.
Abdomen: Smooth tender hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin. No ascites.
Lower limbs: Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin. Calves soft, non-tender. Peripheral pulses present.
Bedside: Blood glucose 8.4 mmol/L. ECG (if requested): atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 110, old Q waves in V1-V3, no acute ST changes.

markingCriteria: Introduces self, obtains consent, explains the examination, ensures privacy and comfort, positions patient at 45 degrees
Performs hand hygiene and a general inspection noting dyspnoea at rest and peripheral signs
Examines the pulse (rate and rhythm) and recognises atrial fibrillation; requests or checks BP
Assesses the JVP correctly and elicits the hepatojugular reflux
Palpates the apex beat and correctly interprets its displacement
Auscultates all valve areas with manoeuvres and identifies the apical pansystolic murmur (likely functional MR)
Examines the chest including percussion and auscultation of the bases; identifies bilateral effusions and crackles
Examines for hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema, and checks the calves
Presents findings succinctly and concludes congestive cardiac failure with AF, likely ischaemic cardiomyopathy, with precipitants (AF, NSAID use)
Lists appropriate investigations: ECG, CXR, FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP, HbA1c, echocardiogram

Outlines initial management: sit up, oxygen to SpO2 target, IV furosemide, fluid balance and daily weights, rate control, anticoagulation assessment (CHA2DS2-VA), stop NSAIDs and hold metformin if renal function deteriorating
Recognises and responds to the social concern about his dependent wife (social work, respite, family contact)
expectedDiagnosis: Decompensated congestive cardiac failure (likely ischaemic cardiomyopathy) precipitated by new atrial fibrillation and NSAID use
teachingPoints: Structure the CVS exam as general inspection, hands, pulse, BP, face, neck (JVP), precordium, back of chest and bases, abdomen (liver), and legs; examiners reward a fluent routine that is explained to the patient.

Always look for the precipitant of decompensated heart failure: arrhythmia (AF), ischaemia, infection, non-adherence, and drugs such as NSAIDs, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers or thiazolidinediones.
Assess stroke risk in AF with CHA2DS2-VA (Australian NHFA/CSANZ AF guidelines drop the sex category); this man scores at least 5 and needs anticoagulation, usually a DOAC.
Guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF (NHFA/CSANZ): ACEI/ARB or ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor, titrated once euvolaemic.
In rural practice, social issues such as a dependent spouse commonly determine whether admission is safe: address them explicitly.

title: New diagnosis of type 2 diabetes
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in Western Sydney. Mrs Priya Nair, a 49-year-old woman, has returned for the results of blood tests done after a routine health check. Her results show fasting glucose 8.9 mmol/L and HbA1c 8.1% (65 mmol/mol) on two occasions two weeks apart. Renal function is normal (eGFR >90), urine ACR 1.8 mg/mmol. BMI 31 kg/m2, BP 136/84 mmHg.

Your tasks are to:
- Explain the diagnosis to Mrs Nair
- Discuss a management plan with her
- Answer her questions
tasks: Explain the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes
Discuss an initial management plan including lifestyle and medication
Address her questions and concerns

patient.name: Priya Nair
patient.persona: Articulate, anxious nurse's aide who has lived in Australia for 15 years. Speaks quickly when nervous, asks many questions. Initially says 'I knew it, I'm going to end up like my mother'. Will only disclose that she works night shifts and skips meals if asked about her routine. Only mentions her fear of needles and amputation if the doctor explores her concerns empathetically.
patient.openingLine: Hi Doctor. The receptionist said you wanted to see me about my bloods. Is it the sugar? My mum had sugar problems.
patient.script:
Background: Attended a health check at her husband's urging. No symptoms she noticed, but on questioning admits to getting up twice a night to pass urine for a few months and feeling thirsty, and has had two episodes of vulval thrush in the past six months. No weight loss. No visual change, no numbness in feet, no chest pain.

PMH: Gestational diabetes in both pregnancies (2004 and 2007), 'they told me to get checked but I never did'. Polycystic ovary syndrome. Mild fatty liver noted on an ultrasound last year.

Meds: Nil regular. Occasional paracetamol. Allergies: nil.

Family history: Mother had type 2 diabetes, on insulin, had a below-knee amputation and died of kidney failure aged 68. Father had a heart attack at 60. Brother has diabetes.

Social: Works as an assistant in nursing at an aged care facility, rotating night shifts four nights a week (HIDDEN CUE 1: she eats biscuits and sweet chai to stay awake and often skips proper meals, sleeps poorly). Married, two teenage children. Never smoked, no alcohol. Vegetarian. Walks very little, 'no time'. Drives.

Ideas: Believes diabetes means she will definitely need insulin injections and lose her legs like her mother. Concerns (HIDDEN CUE 2): Terrified of needles and of 'ending up on dialysis like Mum'; also worried that she will have to stop working night shifts and lose income. Expectations: Wants to know if it can be cured with diet alone, and whether her daughters are at risk.

Questions she will ask: 'Do I need insulin?', 'Will I lose my leg?', 'Can I still work nights?', 'Should my kids be tested?'. She is receptive to a structured plan, and relieved when told that most people start with tablets and that good control greatly reduces complication risk.

markingCriteria: Establishes rapport, checks what she already knows and what she wants to know before giving results
Explains the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes clearly with reference to her two abnormal results, avoiding jargon
Elicits symptoms of hyperglycaemia and relevant history, including previous gestational diabetes and family history
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations, including the fear of insulin, amputation and dialysis based on her mother's experience
Explores lifestyle factors including night-shift work, diet and physical activity
Discusses lifestyle measures: dietitian referral, culturally appropriate diet, 150 minutes a week of physical activity, weight loss target of 5-10%
Offers metformin as first-line pharmacotherapy (explains start low, go slow, GI side effects) and mentions that other agents such as SGLT2 inhibitors may be added
Sets an individualised HbA1c target (generally 7% or 53 mmol/mol or less) per RACGP Management of type 2 diabetes handbook
Addresses cardiovascular risk: BP and lipid assessment, absolute CVD risk calculation, statin consideration
Outlines complication screening and the annual cycle of care: eyes, feet, kidneys (eGFR and ACR), and GP Management Plan with allied health referrals
Mentions NDSS registration, diabetes education, driving considerations if on hypoglycaemic agents, and screening of first-degree relatives
Arranges follow-up and checks understanding (teach-back)
expectedDiagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.1% on repeat testing), with previous gestational diabetes and a strong family history
teachingPoints: In Australia, diabetes can be diagnosed with HbA1c 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more on two occasions in an asymptomatic person, or once with a fasting glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more; MBS allows HbA1c for diagnosis.
Metformin plus lifestyle change is first line; SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists are preferred add-ons when there is established CVD, heart failure or CKD (RACGP/ADS algorithm).
Register every new patient with the NDSS for subsidised supplies and education, and set up a GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement for Medicare-rebated allied health visits.
Women with previous gestational diabetes need screening every 1-3 years for life: missed follow-up is common.
Address the 'my mother lost her leg' fear directly: modern management and early detection substantially reduce the risk of amputation and kidney failure.
Shift workers need tailored advice on meal timing and hypoglycaemia risk if sulfonylureas or insulin are later added.

title: First seizure in a 28-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are an HMO in the emergency department of a metropolitan hospital in Melbourne. Mr Jake Morrison, a 28-year-old man, was brought in by ambulance four hours ago after his partner witnessed a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. He is now fully recovered. His examination is normal. Blood tests (FBC, UEC including sodium, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFT) are normal. Non-contrast CT brain is normal. The neurology registrar has reviewed him and is happy for discharge with outpatient EEG and MRI.

Your tasks are to:
- Explain the likely diagnosis and results to Mr Morrison
- Advise him on safety and driving
- Answer his questions
tasks: Explain the likely diagnosis and the results
Give safety advice, including driving advice
Answer his questions

patient.name: Jake Morrison
patient.persona: Friendly, casual young man ('no worries, when can I get out of here?'). Minimises what happened. Becomes frustrated and a bit argumentative when driving restrictions are mentioned. Will not volunteer his drug use unless asked in a non-judgemental way, and will not mention his work at heights unless asked about his job specifics.
patient.openingLine: Hey Doc. So what's the verdict? My partner reckons I was shaking like crazy but I feel fine now. Can I head home?
patient.script:
Event: Last night at 11 pm, partner Chloe saw him go stiff, cry out, and then jerk all four limbs for about 2 minutes while on the couch. He bit the side of his tongue and was incontinent of urine. Drowsy and confused for 30 minutes afterwards, then slept. No warning he can remember. Never happened before. No recent head injury, fever, headache or neck stiffness. No history of febrile convulsions as a child.

Triggers: He had slept only about 4 hours a night for the past week because of a work deadline and a mate's bucks weekend. HIDDEN CUE 1: If asked non-judgementally about alcohol and drugs, he admits to drinking about 12 beers on each of Friday and Saturday and taking 'a couple of pingers' (MDMA) at the bucks party three days ago; no benzodiazepine use or withdrawal. Drinks less during the week.

PMH: Nil. Meds: Nil. Allergies: Nil.
Family history: Cousin has epilepsy.

Social: Lives with partner in a rented unit. HIDDEN CUE 2: Works as a roof plumber on residential building sites, regularly working on roofs and ladders, and drives the company van to sites every day. Swims at the beach on weekends. Plays in a local footy team.

Ideas: Thinks it was a 'one-off from being run down'. Concerns: Losing his job if he cannot drive; he is the main earner and they have just signed a lease. Expectations: Wants to go home and back to work tomorrow.

Questions: 'Is it epilepsy?', 'Do I need tablets?', 'When can I drive?', 'Can I still go to work?'. If told he cannot drive for six months he says 'That's ridiculous, how am I supposed to get to work?' He calms down if the doctor is empathetic, explains that it is the law and about safety, and offers practical help (medical certificate, talking to employer).

markingCriteria: Introduces self, checks his understanding of the event and what he has been told
Clarifies key features of the episode and possible provoking factors (sleep deprivation, alcohol, recreational drugs) in a non-judgemental way
Explains that this is most likely a first generalised tonic-clonic seizure and that normal bloods and CT are reassuring but do not exclude epilepsy

Explains that a single seizure is not usually diagnosed as epilepsy and that antiseizure medication is not usually started after a first unprovoked seizure; outlines the role of EEG and MRI and neurology follow-up

Gives clear driving advice per Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive: must not drive a private vehicle for a minimum of 6 months after a first seizure, and that commercial vehicle standards are much stricter (years rather than months, decided with the licensing authority)
Explains the patient's legal responsibility to notify the driver licensing authority (VicRoads) and documents the advice
Gives safety advice: no working at heights, ladders or with dangerous machinery, no swimming alone, showers rather than baths, avoid triggers
Advises on reducing alcohol and avoiding recreational drugs and sleep deprivation
Provides seizure first aid information for his partner and when to call 000 (seizure longer than 5 minutes, repeated seizures, injury)
Responds empathetically to his frustration and offers practical support such as a medical certificate and alternative duties at work
Arranges follow-up: GP review, EEG, MRI brain, first seizure clinic, and provides written information (Epilepsy Foundation)
expectedDiagnosis: First generalised tonic-clonic seizure, possibly provoked or lowered threshold by sleep deprivation, alcohol and MDMA use
teachingPoints: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive: after a first seizure, private drivers should not drive for at least 6 months; commercial drivers face much longer non-driving periods, measured in years (the licensing authority decides), and the patient is responsible for notifying the licensing authority.
The doctor documents the advice given; in most states doctors may notify the authority if a patient continues to drive against advice, and South Australia and the NT have mandatory reporting.
After a first unprovoked seizure, around 40% recur within two years; antiseizure medication is usually deferred unless EEG or MRI show a high-risk abnormality.
Occupational and lifestyle safety (heights, water, machinery, bathing) is just as important as driving advice and is commonly missed in the exam.
Always ask about alcohol, recreational drugs (MDMA can cause hyponatraemia and seizures), sleep deprivation and medications that lower the seizure threshold (tramadol, bupropion).

title: Rectal bleeding in a 64-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in a regional town in Victoria. Mr Barry Kowalski, a 64-year-old retired truck driver, has come in because he has noticed blood in his stools. His observations are normal apart from a pulse of 96. He appears pale.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a focused history from Mr Kowalski
- Tell him what you think is going on and your differential diagnosis
- Outline your plan for investigation and referral
tasks: Take a focused history of rectal bleeding and associated symptoms
Explain the differential diagnosis
Outline investigations and referral

patient.name: Barry Kowalski
patient.persona: Embarrassed, gruff older man who finds talking about his bowels awkward ('it's a bit of a delicate one, Doc'). Tries to blame 'piles' and wants cream. Becomes quiet and worried when cancer is raised. Only reveals the unused bowel screening kit and his brother's history if asked specifically.
patient.openingLine: Look, this is a bit embarrassing. I've been getting some blood when I go to the toilet. Probably just piles, but the missus said I should get it looked at.
patient.script:
HPI: Three months of intermittent dark red blood mixed in with the stool, sometimes on the paper too. Not every day, maybe three times a week. Change in bowel habit over four months: previously regular once daily, now looser stools two to three times a day, alternating with a couple of days of constipation. Feels he has not fully emptied (tenesmus). No mucus. Mild crampy left lower abdominal discomfort. HIDDEN CUE 1: Has lost about 6 kg over three months without trying ('the belt's on a new notch'), and feels tired and breathless walking up hills lately. No anal pain, no lump prolapsing, no fever, no nausea or vomiting, no jaundice, no recent antibiotics or travel.

PMH: Hypertension. Gout. Had 'piles' 20 years ago treated with banding. Never had a colonoscopy.

Meds: Amlodipine 5 mg daily, allopurinol 300 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily that he started himself 'for the heart'. No anticoagulants. Allergies: penicillin (rash).

Family history: HIDDEN CUE 2: Younger brother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 52 and had surgery and chemotherapy; he is well now. Mother died of 'stomach cancer' at 70.

Social: Retired long-haul truck driver. Ex-smoker (quit 10 years ago, 35 pack-years). Drinks 3-4 beers daily. Diet high in red and processed meat, 'not much for veggies'. Lives with his wife. Drives. He received three National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kits in the mail over the years and 'chucked them in the drawer'.

Ideas: Thinks it is piles. Concerns: Afraid of a 'camera up the backside', and if pushed, scared it is cancer like his brother. Expectations: Wants a cream and to avoid tests. Accepts colonoscopy if the reason is explained sensitively.

markingCriteria: Puts the patient at ease, acknowledges embarrassment and uses clear non-judgemental language
Characterises the bleeding: colour, amount, relation to stool, frequency, duration
Asks about change in bowel habit, tenesmus, mucus, abdominal pain and anal symptoms
Elicits red flag features: unintentional weight loss, fatigue and symptoms of anaemia
Takes a family history and identifies the brother's early-onset bowel cancer
Asks about previous screening (NBCSP) and colonoscopy
Takes a medication history including aspirin and anticoagulants, and allergies
Covers social risk factors: smoking, alcohol, diet
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations sensitively
Explains that colorectal cancer must be excluded; gives a sensible differential (haemorrhoids, diverticular disease, IBD, polyps)

Plans DRE and abdominal examination, FBC, iron studies, UEC, LFTs, CEA not as a screening test, and urgent colonoscopy referral (within 30 days per Optimal Care Pathway), with safety-netting for heavy bleeding
Recommends that he should not use an FOBT now because he is symptomatic, and that his family history also affects relatives' screening
expectedDiagnosis: Suspected colorectal carcinoma (left-sided/rectosigmoid) with probable iron deficiency anaemia; differentials haemorrhoids, diverticular disease, IBD
teachingPoints: Rectal bleeding in a person over 50, or with change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron deficiency anaemia or a strong family history, needs colonoscopy, not a trial of haemorrhoid cream.
The iFOBT through the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program is for asymptomatic people aged 45-74 every two years; symptomatic patients go straight to diagnostic colonoscopy.
The Cancer Council Optimal Care Pathway for colorectal cancer recommends colonoscopy within 30 days for suspected cancer, sooner if significant bleeding or anaemia.

A first-degree relative diagnosed under 55 puts the patient in a higher risk category (NHMRC/Cancer Council guidelines): colonoscopy every five years from age 45 or 10 years before the relative's diagnosis; offer cascade advice for his children.
Men find these consultations embarrassing: acknowledge it, ask directly, and explain procedures in plain language.

title: Groin lump in a 55-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in a suburban clinic in Perth. Mr Tony Russo, a 55-year-old warehouse worker, has noticed a lump in his right groin for two months. It is not painful at present.

Your tasks are to:
- Examine Mr Russo's groin, explaining what you are doing; the examiner will give you your findings
- Explain the findings and the most likely diagnosis to Mr Russo
- Discuss management and advice
tasks: Perform an examination of the groin and scrotum
Explain the findings and the most likely diagnosis
Discuss management and safety-netting

patient.name: Tony Russo
patient.persona: Friendly, talkative man who jokes to hide embarrassment about being examined. Keen to avoid surgery because he cannot afford time off. Only reveals that he has had one episode where the lump became painful and would not go back if asked about episodes of pain or trouble pushing it back.
patient.openingLine: G'day Doc. I've got this lump down there in the groin. The wife reckons it's a hernia. Not really hurting, just a bit of a drag at the end of the day.
patient.script:
HPI: Two months of a right groin lump, noticed after lifting heavy boxes at work. Bigger at the end of the day and when he coughs or strains, disappears when he lies down. Dragging ache, 3/10, worse after lifting. HIDDEN CUE 1: Two weeks ago the lump became painful and would not go back for about an hour after a heavy lift; he felt a bit sick, then it went back when he lay in a warm bath. He did not seek help. No vomiting, bowels normal, passing wind, no urinary symptoms, no testicular pain or swelling, no weight loss, no fever.

PMH: COPD, mild, with a chronic smoker's cough. Benign prostatic hypertrophy with some straining to pass urine. No previous surgery.

Meds: Tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol as needed. Allergies: nil.

Family: Father had 'hernias on both sides'.

Social: Forklift driver and warehouse worker, lifts up to 25 kg regularly. Smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Two to three beers a night. Married, lives with wife. Drives. Casual employee: 'if I'm off, I don't get paid'.

Ideas: Thinks it is a hernia. Concerns: Time off work and income. HIDDEN CUE 2: Worried it could be cancer because a mate had a 'lump in the groin that turned out to be lymphoma', only shared if asked what worries him. Expectations: Hopes it can be 'left alone' or managed with a truss.
patient.examFindings:
General: Well man, BMI approximately 29. Examined standing first, then supine.
Inspection standing: Visible 4 cm swelling in the right groin, above and medial to the pubic tubercle, extending towards the top of the scrotum. No skin changes, no scars. Left groin normal.
Cough impulse: Positive expansile cough impulse over the right swelling.
Palpation: Soft, non-tender, 4 x 3 cm swelling. Cannot get above it in the scrotum. Lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle. Reducible on lying down with gentle pressure; with the patient lying and the deep inguinal ring (midpoint of the inguinal ligament) occluded, the swelling does not reappear on coughing; it reappears when pressure is released.
Transillumination: Negative.
Scrotum and testes: Both testes palpable, normal size and consistency, separate from the swelling. No varicocele.
Lymph nodes: No inguinal lymphadenopathy.
Other: Left side normal on cough. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses, no organomegaly. Normal bowel sounds. Examiner will state that a DRE is not required.

markingCriteria: Introduces self, gains consent, explains the need for exposure, offers a chaperone and ensures privacy
Examines with the patient standing first, inspecting both groins and scrotum
Tests the cough impulse on both sides
Palpates the lump, establishing relationship to the pubic tubercle, whether one can get above it, consistency, tenderness and reducibility
Examines the testes and scrotum, and checks for transillumination
Performs the deep ring occlusion test with the patient lying down and interprets it correctly
Examines the contralateral side, inguinal lymph nodes and abdomen, and mentions checking for contributing factors (chronic cough, prostatism)
Correctly concludes a reducible right indirect inguinal hernia and explains it in simple language
Identifies the recent episode of incarceration and explains that this raises the risk of strangulation
Recommends referral for elective surgical repair (open or laparoscopic mesh repair) rather than a truss, with a reasonably prompt referral given the episode
Gives clear safety-netting: attend ED immediately if the lump becomes painful, tense, irreducible, or with vomiting or abdominal distension
Addresses modifiable factors (smoking cessation, weight, lifting technique), work issues and his concern about cancer
expectedDiagnosis: Right reducible indirect inguinal hernia with a recent episode of transient incarceration
teachingPoints: Inguinal hernias arise above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernias arise below and lateral to it and have a higher risk of strangulation.
Controlling the deep ring after reduction helps distinguish indirect from direct hernias, but clinical distinction is unreliable; the key decision is referral for repair.
Symptomatic hernias, or any history of incarceration, should be referred for elective repair; watchful waiting is only reasonable for minimally symptomatic hernias in men.
Always safety-net for strangulation: pain, tenderness, irreducibility, vomiting and obstruction require urgent ED attendance.
Look for and address contributors to raised intra-abdominal pressure: chronic cough, constipation, prostatism, obesity and heavy lifting.
In Australia, workers may be eligible for workers' compensation if the hernia is related to lifting at work: mention it for a casual labourer worried about income.

title: Motorbike crash in a 32-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are the senior medical officer on duty in the emergency department of a rural hospital in Mount Isa, Queensland. There is no on-site surgeon; the nearest trauma centre is in Townsville (retrieval by RFDS). Mr Dylan Carter, a 32-year-old man, has been brought in by ambulance after coming off his motorbike at about 80 km/h on a dirt road. Paramedics have applied a cervical collar. A nurse is with you.

Your tasks are to:
- Assess and manage Mr Carter, telling the examiner what you are doing and asking for findings as you go
- Tell the examiner your working diagnosis
- Outline your ongoing plan
tasks: Perform a structured primary survey with simultaneous resuscitation
State the working diagnosis
Outline ongoing management and retrieval

patient.name: Dylan Carter
patient.persona: In pain, anxious and increasingly drowsy and short-tempered as the station goes on. Speaks in short phrases ('me chest, mate, it's killing me'). Answers simple questions. Asks repeatedly about his bike and whether he is going to be okay. Will only tell you he takes a blood thinner if asked about medications (AMPLE history).
patient.openingLine: Argh, me chest... I can't get a proper breath. Is me bike alright?
patient.script:
Mechanism: Came off his trail bike at about 80 km/h on a corrugated dirt road about 90 minutes ago, hit a tree with his left side. Helmet on, no leathers. Brief loss of consciousness per his mate. Paramedics: GCS 14 on scene, gave methoxyflurane and 10 mg IV morphine.

Symptoms: Severe left chest pain worse on breathing, left upper abdominal pain, pain in the left thigh. Some neck pain. No numbness or weakness in limbs.

AMPLE: Allergies: none. HIDDEN CUE 1: Medications: apixaban 5 mg twice daily for a DVT three months ago after a knee reconstruction (only revealed if asked). Past history: knee reconstruction; otherwise well. Last meal: pie and a can of Coke four hours ago. Events: as above.

Social: Mine worker on a fly-in fly-out roster. Smokes. Drinks on days off: had 'a few beers' before riding (HIDDEN CUE 2: admits to 6 beers if asked directly). Lives with partner.

Course if managed correctly: If needle or finger decompression and then an intercostal catheter (chest drain) is placed on the left, breathing and oxygen saturation improve. If he receives warmed blood and permissive hypotensive resuscitation, BP improves temporarily to about 100 systolic then drifts again (ongoing splenic bleeding). If the candidate does not decompress the chest, he becomes more hypoxic and hypotensive.

Concerns: Wants to know if he will be okay and asks the team to call his partner. Expectations: Wants pain relief.
patient.examFindings:
Airway: Talking in short phrases, airway patent. Cervical collar in place; C-spine tenderness in the midline at C5-6 on log roll.
Breathing: RR 32, SpO2 86% on 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask. Trachea deviated to the right. Reduced chest expansion on the left. Hyperresonant percussion on the left. Absent breath sounds on the left. Tender left lower ribs with crepitus. After decompression and chest drain: RR 24, SpO2 95%, rush of air, then 200 mL blood in the drain.
Circulation: HR 128, BP 88/54 mmHg, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds. Distended neck veins before decompression. Abdomen: tender left upper quadrant with guarding. Pelvis: stable on gentle single compression, no deformity. Left thigh swollen and deformed, distal pulses present. eFAST (if requested): free fluid in the splenorenal space; no pericardial effusion; absent lung sliding on the left before the drain.
Disability: GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6), pupils equal and reactive 3 mm. Moves all four limbs. BGL 6.2 mmol/L.
Exposure: Temperature 35.4 C. Abrasions to left flank and arm. Closed deformity of the left mid-thigh.
Investigations (if requested): Hb 102 g/L, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, VBG pH 7.29, BE -6. Coagulation pending. Bedside CXR after drain: re-expanded left lung, fractured left ribs 8-10. Pelvic X-ray: normal. Blood alcohol pending.

markingCriteria: Calls for help early (trauma team, senior advice, RFDS/retrieval coordination), uses a structured approach and wears PPE
Assesses airway with cervical spine protection and maintains spinal precautions
Recognises tension pneumothorax clinically, without waiting for imaging, and performs immediate needle or finger decompression followed by an intercostal catheter
Gives high flow oxygen and reassesses breathing after each intervention
Establishes two large-bore IV cannulas, sends bloods including crossmatch, coagulation and VBG, and recognises haemorrhagic shock
Uses permissive hypotension and early blood products (activates massive transfusion protocol, considers tranexamic acid within 3 hours), avoiding large volumes of crystalloid
Identifies the intra-abdominal bleeding (splenic injury on eFAST) and the need for definitive surgical control
Elicits the anticoagulant (apixaban) in the AMPLE history and plans reversal (andexanet alfa if available, or prothrombin complex concentrate) with haematology advice
Assesses disability (GCS, pupils, glucose) and exposure, prevents hypothermia, and splints the femoral fracture (traction splint) with adequate analgesia
States the working diagnosis: multi-trauma with left tension pneumothorax, haemorrhagic shock from likely splenic injury, femoral fracture, possible cervical spine injury
Plans urgent retrieval to a major trauma centre, communicates clearly using ISBAR, and documents
Communicates with the patient compassionately, gives analgesia and offers to contact his partner
expectedDiagnosis: Multi-trauma: left tension pneumothorax with rib fractures, haemorrhagic shock from probable splenic injury, closed left femoral shaft fracture, possible cervical spine injury, in an anticoagulated patient
teachingPoints: Follow the EMST (ATLS) primary survey: Airway with C-spine control, Breathing, Circulation with haemorrhage control, Disability, Exposure; treat life threats as you find them.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: decompress immediately (finger thoracostomy or needle in the 4th/5th intercostal space mid-axillary line in adults) then insert an intercostal catheter; do not wait for a CXR.

Damage control resuscitation: permissive hypotension (systolic around 80-90 mmHg in the absence of head injury), early blood and plasma via massive transfusion protocol, tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2).
The AMPLE history matters: DOACs dramatically change the management of traumatic haemorrhage; reversal is with andexanet alfa (factor Xa inhibitors) or PCC, and idarucizumab for dabigatran.

In rural Australia, early activation of retrieval (RFDS, state retrieval service) is part of resuscitation; stabilise, communicate with ISBAR and transfer, rather than attempting definitive surgery without resources.
A femoral shaft fracture can lose 1-1.5 L of blood: splint early for pain and haemorrhage control.

title: Lower abdominal pain and spotting in early pregnancy
candidateBrief:
You are an HMO in the emergency department of a metropolitan hospital in Adelaide. Ms Jasmine Taylor, a 26-year-old woman, has presented with lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was seven weeks ago. A urine pregnancy test in triage is positive. Observations: BP 104/66 mmHg, HR 102, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9 C.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a focused history from Ms Taylor
- Explain the likely diagnosis and your differentials
- Outline your immediate management plan
tasks: Take a focused history of pain and bleeding in early pregnancy
Explain the likely diagnosis and differentials
Outline the immediate management plan

patient.name: Jasmine Taylor
patient.persona: Anxious, in pain, speaks softly and hesitates when asked about relationships. Says 'I didn't even know I was pregnant until today'. Answers direct questions. Only discloses her concerns about her partner if the doctor asks about safety at home privately and gently.
patient.openingLine: I've got this really bad pain down on the right side and I've been spotting. The nurse just told me I'm pregnant. I didn't even know.
patient.script:
HPI: Right iliac fossa pain started 12 hours ago, initially crampy, now constant and sharp, 7/10. Some pain at the tip of the right shoulder for the last two hours (only if asked). Brown-red spotting for two days, less than a period, no clots, no tissue passed. HIDDEN CUE 1: Felt dizzy and nearly fainted on the toilet this morning. Nausea, no vomiting. Mild urge to open bowels. No fever, no urinary symptoms, no vaginal discharge.

Gynae: LMP seven weeks ago, periods usually regular every 28 days. Pregnancy not planned. Contraception: had a copper IUD inserted three years ago (still in place, she thinks). Past chlamydia infection two years ago, treated. Cervical screening done last year, normal. G1 P0.

PMH: Nil else. Meds: nil. Allergies: nil. Blood group: does not know.

Social: Works in a café. Smokes 10 a day. Drinks socially. Lives with her partner, Kyle, 29, for 18 months.

HIDDEN CUE 2 (only if asked about safety at home, ideally with her partner out of the room): Kyle gets angry and 'grabs me sometimes'; he pushed her into a wall last month. He checks her phone and controls the money. She is scared of how he will react to the pregnancy. No children. Would like information but is not ready to leave.

Ideas: Thinks she might be losing the baby. Concerns: Whether she will need surgery and whether she can have children later; how Kyle will react. Expectations: Wants pain relief and to know what is going on. Wants to keep this confidential from Kyle for now.

markingCriteria: Introduces self, acknowledges pain and distress and offers analgesia early
Characterises the pain (site, onset, nature, severity, radiation including shoulder tip pain) and bleeding
Elicits symptoms of haemodynamic compromise (presyncope) and recognises the tachycardia and borderline BP
Takes a menstrual, obstetric and contraceptive history, identifying the IUD
Identifies risk factors for ectopic pregnancy: previous chlamydia (PID), IUD in situ, smoking
Asks about gynaecological history, cervical screening and STI history sensitively
Asks about safety at home in a private, non-judgemental way and responds appropriately to the disclosure of family violence
States ruptured or leaking ectopic pregnancy as the most likely diagnosis with sensible differentials (threatened/incomplete miscarriage, ruptured corpus luteum cyst, appendicitis, ovarian torsion)
Outlines immediate management: two large-bore cannulas, FBC, group and hold/crossmatch, quantitative beta-hCG, urgent transvaginal ultrasound, urgent gynaecology review, keep nil by mouth
Mentions anti-D immunoglobulin if Rh negative
Explains likely need for surgery (laparoscopy, possible salpingectomy) and addresses fertility concern honestly
Offers support for family violence: safety planning, social work, 1800RESPECT, and respects confidentiality
expectedDiagnosis: Suspected ruptured (leaking) right ectopic pregnancy with early haemodynamic compromise; disclosure of intimate partner violence
teachingPoints: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain or PV bleeding needs a pregnancy test; a positive test with pain and bleeding is ectopic until proven otherwise.
Shoulder tip pain, presyncope, tachycardia and peritonism suggest haemoperitoneum: resuscitate and get urgent gynaecology review and theatre, rather than waiting for serial beta-hCG.
Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy include previous PID or chlamydia, tubal surgery, previous ectopic, IVF, IUD in situ (fewer pregnancies overall but a higher proportion are ectopic) and smoking.
Give anti-D (250 IU in the first trimester) to Rh D negative women with ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage requiring surgical management (NBA/RANZCOG guidance).
Pregnancy is a high-risk time for the onset or escalation of intimate partner violence; ask routinely and privately, and link to support (1800RESPECT, social work, safety planning).
After salpingectomy with a healthy contralateral tube, most women can still conceive naturally: this is the usual fertility question.

title: Gestational diabetes result at 26 weeks
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner providing shared antenatal care in a clinic in Canberra. Mrs Mei Lin Chen, a 34-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 26 weeks' gestation, has come for the results of her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Results: fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.6 mmol/L, 2-hour 8.2 mmol/L. Her booking bloods and morphology scan were normal. BMI at booking was 27 kg/m2. BP today 118/72 mmHg.

Your tasks are to:
- Explain the result and the diagnosis to Mrs Chen
- Discuss the implications for her and her baby
- Outline the management plan
tasks: Explain the OGTT result and the diagnosis
Discuss the implications for mother and baby
Outline the management plan and follow-up

patient.name: Mei Lin Chen
patient.persona: Well-educated accountant, calm on the surface but visibly worried. Asks precise questions and likes numbers. Feels guilty: 'Did I cause this by eating too much rice?'. Only mentions that she has stopped eating properly since reading about it online if asked what she has been eating in the last few days.
patient.openingLine: Hi Doctor. The lab called and said I need to come in for my glucose test result. Is something wrong with the baby?
patient.script:
Pregnancy: G1 P0, 26 weeks, conceived naturally, planned. Dating scan and morphology scan normal. Feeling baby move well. No headaches, visual disturbance, swelling, bleeding or abdominal pain. No urinary symptoms.

PMH: Nil significant. No previous glucose testing. Meds: Pregnancy multivitamin with folate and iodine. Allergies: nil.

Family history: Father has type 2 diabetes. Mother had 'high sugar' in pregnancy.

Social: Born in Shanghai, moved to Australia 10 years ago. Accountant, desk-based, long hours during tax season. Non-smoker, no alcohol since pregnancy. Lives with husband David. Diet is mainly rice, noodles and dumplings; drinks bubble tea two or three times a week. Walks little.

HIDDEN CUE 1: Since the lab call two days ago she has read online that sugar harms the baby and has been skipping meals and eating almost no carbohydrate; she felt shaky and light-headed at work yesterday (only if asked about recent diet or how she has been feeling).

Ideas: Thinks she caused it by eating badly. Concerns: That the baby will be 'damaged' or that she will need insulin needles, and (HIDDEN CUE 2, only if asked about longer-term worries) that she will end up with diabetes like her father. Expectations: Wants to know exactly what to eat and whether she can still have a normal birth.

Questions she will ask: 'Is my baby okay?', 'Will I need insulin?', 'Will I need a caesarean?', 'Will it go away after birth?', 'Can I still breastfeed?'. She responds well to reassurance, a clear plan, and being told it is not her fault.

markingCriteria: Establishes rapport, checks her understanding and explains the purpose of the OGTT
Interprets the result correctly: fasting 5.4 (threshold 5.1) and 1-hour 10.6 (threshold 10.0) meet ADIPS/WHO criteria; one abnormal value is sufficient
Explains gestational diabetes in plain language and addresses guilt (placental hormones cause insulin resistance, not her fault)
Explains fetal and neonatal risks: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, polyhydramnios, stillbirth risk if uncontrolled
Explains maternal risks: pre-eclampsia, caesarean, and future type 2 diabetes
Identifies the unsafe restrictive eating and hypoglycaemic symptoms, and corrects it with advice on balanced, regular carbohydrate intake

Outlines management: referral to the hospital diabetes-in-pregnancy team, dietitian and diabetes educator, NDSS registration, home glucose monitoring (fasting and 1 or 2 hours post meals) with targets
Explains that medication (metformin or insulin) is needed if targets are not met with lifestyle measures
Discusses monitoring: growth ultrasound, BP and urine checks, and timing of birth guided by the obstetric team
Explains postpartum plan: breastfeeding encouraged, glucose checks for the baby, 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum and then diabetes screening every 1-3 years
Checks understanding, answers questions and arranges follow-up
expectedDiagnosis: Gestational diabetes mellitus (fasting 5.4 and 1-hour 10.6 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT)
teachingPoints: ADIPS/WHO 2013 criteria (used in Australia): 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks; GDM if fasting 5.1-6.9, 1-hour 10.0 or higher, or 2-hour 8.5-11.0 mmol/L. One abnormal value is enough.
Typical capillary glucose targets: fasting 5.0 mmol/L or less (some services 5.3), 1-hour post-prandial 7.4 or less, 2-hour 6.7 or less.
Most women are managed with diet and activity; metformin or insulin are added if targets are not met. Registration with the NDSS gives subsidised monitoring supplies.
Postpartum follow-up is often missed: OGTT 6-12 weeks after birth, then screening every 1-3 years, and early testing in future pregnancies.
Women of Asian, Indian subcontinent, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Pacific Islander and Middle Eastern background are at higher risk of GDM.
Always check whether the patient has responded to a new diagnosis with unsafe behaviour such as severe carbohydrate restriction.

title: Abnormal cervical screening result
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in a clinic in Hobart. Ms Kate Brennan, a 31-year-old woman, has come to discuss the result of her routine Cervical Screening Test, which she collected herself (self-collected vaginal swab) three weeks ago. The result reads: Oncogenic HPV type 16 detected. Her last screening test, five years ago, was normal.

Your tasks are to:
- Explain the result to Ms Brennan
- Explain the next steps
- Address her concerns
tasks: Explain the HPV 16 result
Explain the next steps, including colposcopy
Address her concerns and questions

patient.name: Kate Brennan
patient.persona: Chatty, quite anxious primary school teacher who has googled 'HPV 16' and is frightened it means cancer. Speaks fast, uses Australian expressions ('I've been absolutely freaking out'). Becomes tearful when talking about her relationship. Only reveals that she has had intermenstrual and post-coital bleeding if asked specifically about bleeding.
patient.openingLine: Hi. So I got a text saying my result was ready and I looked it up and it says HPV 16 and now I'm totally freaking out. Have I got cancer?
patient.script:
Background: Did a self-collected swab because she finds speculum exams uncomfortable. Previous test five years ago was normal (HPV not detected). HPV vaccination: she was in Year 8 in 2008 but missed some school vaccination days, so she thinks she only had one of the three doses and is not sure.

Symptoms: HIDDEN CUE 1 (only if asked about bleeding): Two months of occasional spotting after sex and between periods. No abnormal discharge, no pelvic pain, no weight loss. Periods regular.

Gynae: G0. Combined oral contraceptive pill for 10 years. No previous STIs, last STI screen three years ago.

PMH: Nil. Meds: COCP (levonorgestrel/ethinylestradiol). Allergies: nil.

Social: Teacher. Non-smoker. Drinks on weekends. In a relationship with her partner Sam for four years.

HIDDEN CUE 2 (only if asked about her concerns or relationship with empathy): She is worried that HPV means Sam has been unfaithful, or that he will think she has. She had two other partners before Sam. She is afraid this will end the relationship. Also worried about whether she can have children because they plan to start trying next year.

Ideas: Thinks HPV 16 means she has cancer. Concerns: Cancer, infidelity, fertility, and that she 'did something wrong'. Expectations: Wants to know if she needs surgery and whether Sam needs a test.

She calms down significantly if told HPV is extremely common, that most infections clear, that it can be dormant for years so it does not indicate infidelity, and that colposcopy is to look for and treat any pre-cancerous change early.

markingCriteria: Establishes what she knows and her main worry before explaining the result
Explains HPV in plain language: very common, sexually transmitted, most infections clear within 1-2 years, and HPV 16/18 carries a higher risk of pre-cancerous change
Clearly states that the result does not mean she has cancer
Asks about symptoms, specifically post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding, and recognises their significance
Explains the National Cervical Screening Program pathway: HPV 16/18 detected needs direct referral to colposcopy regardless of cytology
Explains that because the sample was self-collected, a clinician-collected sample for liquid-based cytology is taken at colposcopy (or can be collected now)
Recognises that abnormal bleeding needs a speculum examination and prompt specialist assessment, regardless of screening results
Explains colposcopy: what happens, that it is usually done without an anaesthetic, and possible treatment (LLETZ) if high-grade changes are found
Addresses fertility: small increased risk of preterm birth after LLETZ, not usually affecting ability to conceive
Addresses the infidelity concern sensitively: HPV can persist undetected for many years, so it does not indicate recent infidelity; partners are not routinely tested
Discusses HPV vaccination status and offers STI screening
Offers written information, safety-nets and arranges follow-up of the colposcopy result
expectedDiagnosis: Oncogenic HPV 16 detected on cervical screening, with symptoms of post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding; requires colposcopy
teachingPoints: Australia's National Cervical Screening Program uses a primary HPV test every 5 years for people with a cervix aged 25-74; self-collection is available to everyone eligible since July 2022.
HPV 16/18 detected on any sample means direct referral for colposcopy; other oncogenic HPV types are triaged by cytology.
A self-collected sample cannot be used for cytology, so reflex cytology needs a clinician-collected sample at or before colposcopy.
Screening tests are for asymptomatic people: post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding needs a clinical examination and co-test regardless of the screening result.
HPV can remain latent for years; reassure about infidelity concerns, and remember that condoms reduce but do not eliminate transmission.
HPV vaccination in Australia (Gardasil 9) is now a single dose in the school program at age 12-13; catch-up is free up to age 25 under the NIP.

title: Febrile seizure in an 18-month-old
candidateBrief:
You are an HMO in the paediatric emergency department of a hospital in Newcastle, NSW. Ms Sarah O'Brien is the mother of Oliver, an 18-month-old boy who had a seizure at home two hours ago. The registrar found a 2-minute generalised seizure with a temperature of 39.2 C, due to a viral upper respiratory tract infection, with no signs of meningitis. He is now playing and drinking. The registrar has diagnosed a simple febrile seizure and he is being discharged.

Your tasks are to:
- Explain the diagnosis to Ms O'Brien
- Advise her on managing fever and what to do if it happens again
- Address her concerns
tasks: Explain the diagnosis of simple febrile seizure
Advise on fever management and seizure first aid
Address her concerns and safety-net

patient.name: Sarah O'Brien
patient.persona: Mother, shaken and tearful at first ('I honestly thought he was dying'). Speaks quickly, asks the same question in different ways. Calms with clear explanation. Only reveals the family history of epilepsy and her plan to sit up all night if asked directly about her worries or what she plans to do at home.
patient.openingLine: Is he going to be okay? I've never seen anything like it. His eyes rolled back and he was shaking all over and he went all blue around the lips. I thought he was dying.
patient.script:
The event (about Oliver): This afternoon he had a runny nose and felt hot. At 4 pm, while on the couch, he suddenly went stiff, his eyes rolled back and all four limbs jerked for about 2 minutes (she timed it on her phone). Lips went a bit blue. Afterwards he was sleepy for about 20 minutes, then woke and was grizzly but moving everything. First ever episode. She called 000. Temperature 39.2 C at triage. No rash, no neck stiffness, no vomiting, drinking well, several wet nappies.

Oliver's background: Born at term, normal delivery, no neonatal problems. Development normal: walking, says about 10 words. Immunisations up to date including 18-month vaccines two weeks ago. No medications, no allergies. Attends childcare three days a week.

Family history: HIDDEN CUE 1: Her younger brother had febrile seizures as a toddler, and Oliver's father's cousin has epilepsy. She is worried Oliver now has epilepsy.

Social: Lives with partner Ben (works FIFO, currently away) and Oliver. She is a nurse's assistant. No other children; she is 12 weeks pregnant.

Ideas: Thinks the seizure might have caused brain damage, or that it means epilepsy. Concerns: That it will happen again tonight and she will be alone; whether the 18-month vaccines caused it; whether she should stop childcare. HIDDEN CUE 2: Plans to give him paracetamol and ibuprofen around the clock and stay awake all night watching him, and has been bundling him in blankets because 'he was shivering'.

Expectations: Wants to know if he needs tests or medicine to stop it happening again. She asks: 'Will this happen again?', 'Has it damaged his brain?', 'Is it epilepsy?', 'Was it the vaccine?', 'What do I do if it happens again?'.

markingCriteria: Acknowledges her distress with empathy and checks her understanding before explaining

Explains simple febrile seizure in plain language: a seizure triggered by fever in a child aged 6 months to 5 years, lasting under 15 minutes, generalised, not recurring within 24 hours, with full recovery
Reassures that simple febrile seizures do not cause brain damage and do not affect development or intelligence
Gives accurate recurrence risk (about 30%, higher if under 18 months or with a family history) and explains the risk of later epilepsy is only slightly higher than the general population
Explains that no EEG, brain scan or antiseizure medication is needed, and that antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures
Advises on fever management for comfort only: paracetamol or ibuprofen if the child is distressed, fluids, light clothing, and not to over-bundle or give medicines around the clock
Teaches seizure first aid: stay calm, place on side on a safe surface, nothing in the mouth, time it, call 000 if it lasts over 5 minutes, recurs, or he does not recover
Addresses the vaccine question accurately and encourages continuing immunisations
Gives safety-netting for signs of serious illness: rash, neck stiffness, drowsiness, poor feeding, breathing difficulty
Addresses the practical and emotional concern of being alone tonight, and offers support (family or friend, follow-up with the GP)
Provides written information (for example the RCH Melbourne or Sydney Children's Hospitals fact sheet) and arranges GP follow-up
expectedDiagnosis: Simple febrile seizure secondary to a viral upper respiratory tract infection
teachingPoints: Simple febrile seizures: generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, age 6 months to 5 years, full recovery; complex features (focal, prolonged, repeated) need further assessment.
Around 30% recur, most within a year; risk factors include onset under 18 months, family history, lower temperature at seizure, and short duration of fever before the seizure.
Antipyretics are for comfort and do not prevent recurrence (RCH clinical practice guidelines); do not recommend alternating regimens around the clock.
Investigations are guided by the cause of the fever, not the seizure; EEG and neuroimaging are not indicated after a simple febrile seizure.
Vaccines can cause fever and therefore occasionally a febrile seizure, but this is not a contraindication to further vaccines; reassure and encourage completion of the NIP schedule.
Parents remember first aid: teach recovery position, timing, and when to call 000.

title: Barking cough in a 3-year-old at night

You are an HMO in the emergency department of a rural hospital in Bundaberg, Queensland, at 2 am. Mr Liam Walker has brought in his 3-year-old son Noah, who woke with a harsh barking cough and noisy breathing. Triage observations: HR 130, RR 36, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.1 C, weight 15 kg.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a brief focused history from Mr Walker
- Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
- Explain the diagnosis and outline your management plan to Mr Walker

Request and interpret the relevant examination findings
Explain the diagnosis and management plan

patient.name: Liam Walker
patient.persona: Father, tired and worried, a bit gruff ('he sounds like a seal, mate'). Respectful but wants action. Relaxes as things are explained. Does not mention his worry about the family's older child with asthma, or that they live 45 minutes out of town, unless asked about home or going home.
patient.openingLine: Doc, he woke up an hour ago barking like a seal and making this horrible noise when he breathes in. It's really scaring me.
patient.script:
About Noah: Runny nose and mild fever for two days, otherwise well and playing. Woke at 1 am with a barking cough, hoarse voice and a harsh noise on breathing in. Has improved slightly in the cold night air on the drive in. Drinking okay, three wet nappies yesterday. Not drooling, can swallow fine, talking and crying normally (hoarse). No choking episode, not playing with small objects before this (only if asked about foreign body). No rash, no vomiting.
