Family and social: Lives with partner Emma, Noah and 6-year-old daughter Ruby, who has asthma. Liam is a sugar cane farmer. Nobody smokes inside, but Liam smokes outside. HIDDEN CUE 1: They live on a property 45 minutes from the hospital and Emma has the other car in Brisbane until tomorrow; Liam worries about getting back quickly if Noah gets worse.

Ideas: Thinks he may have 'something stuck' or 'the asthma like his sister'. Concerns: Whether Noah can breathe properly, whether he needs a tube in his throat. Expectations: Wants to know if they can go home tonight.

HIDDEN CUE 2: Liam has been giving Noah some of Ruby's salbutamol puffer at home (only if asked what he has tried).
patient.examFindings:
General: Alert, sitting on father's lap, interactive and consolable, not toxic. Hoarse cry. Not drooling, no tripod positioning.
Respiratory: Inspiratory stridor at rest when upset, disappears when settled. Mild suprasternal and subcostal recession. RR 36. SpO2 96% on room air. Good air entry bilaterally. No wheeze, no crackles.
Colour: Pink, no cyanosis.
Conscious state: Alert.
ENT: Mild pharyngeal erythema. Do not examine the throat with a tongue depressor if epiglottitis is suspected (the examiner will prompt that this is unnecessary here).
Cardiovascular: HR 130, capillary refill under 2 seconds, well hydrated.
Other: No rash, no lymphadenopathy of note, neck supple.
Reassessment 30 minutes after oral dexamethasone (if given): Stridor only when crying, no recession, settled.
Reassessment at 3-4 hours: No stridor at rest, playing, drinking.

markingCriteria: Introduces self, engages both father and child, keeps the child calm on the parent's lap and avoids distressing interventions
Takes a focused history: onset, prodrome, barking cough, stridor, fever, drooling, swallowing, choking or foreign body, previous episodes, immunisation (Hib)
Identifies what has been given at home, including the sister's salbutamol
Requests the key examination findings: stridor at rest, work of breathing, colour, conscious state, SpO2, toxicity
Correctly grades severity as moderate croup (stridor at rest when upset, mild recession)
Excludes important differentials: epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, foreign body, anaphylaxis
Prescribes oral dexamethasone 0.15-0.3 mg/kg (or prednisolone 1 mg/kg), with dose calculated for 15 kg
States that nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup and explains observation after it; notes that salbutamol has no role
Explains the diagnosis to the father in plain language and addresses his concerns
Plans observation and reassessment, with discharge only if no stridor at rest, considering distance from hospital and access to transport
Gives clear safety-netting: return or call 000 for stridor at rest, increasing work of breathing, drooling, colour change or drowsiness
Offers brief smoking cessation advice and a follow-up plan with the GP
teachingPoints: Croup is usually parainfluenza-driven, peaks at 6 months to 3 years, and presents with barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, typically worse at night.

All children with croup who need to see a doctor should get oral steroid: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (up to 0.3-0.6 mg/kg for more severe) or prednisolone 1 mg/kg (RCH and Queensland Children's guidelines).
Nebulised adrenaline (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, up to 5 mL) is for severe croup; observe for at least 3-4 hours afterwards because of rebound.
Salbutamol, antibiotics, humidified air and steam have no role.
Red flags for other diagnoses: drooling, toxic appearance, muffled voice, inability to swallow (epiglottitis, tracheitis), sudden onset with choking (foreign body).
In rural practice, the discharge decision must account for distance, transport and time of night: a low threshold to observe overnight is appropriate.

title: Unexplained leg injury in a 5-month-old
candidateBrief:
You are an HMO in the emergency department of a regional hospital in Townsville, Queensland. Ms Kayla Nguyen has brought in her 5-month-old daughter, Ruby, because she has been crying and not moving her left leg since this morning. An X-ray shows a spiral fracture of the left femoral shaft. The triage nurse noticed a small bruise on Ruby's cheek. Ruby is otherwise well, with a normal temperature.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a history from Ms Nguyen
- Explain to Ms Nguyen what needs to happen next
- Tell the examiner your assessment and the steps you would take
tasks: Take a history of the injury and relevant background
Explain the next steps to the parent
Tell the examiner your assessment and child protection actions

patient.name: Kayla Nguyen
patient.persona: Young mother, exhausted and defensive. Gives vague and slightly changing answers about how the injury happened. Becomes upset and angry if she feels accused ('Are you saying I hurt my baby?'). Softens if the doctor stays calm, non-judgemental and focused on Ruby's wellbeing. Only discloses her partner's behaviour and her own low mood if asked privately and gently about home and support.
patient.openingLine: She's been screaming all morning and she won't move her leg. I don't know what happened, she was fine last night.
patient.script:
Account of injury: Initially says 'I don't know, she was fine last night'. If asked again, says 'maybe she got her leg stuck in the cot bars'. Later says her partner Josh 'might have rolled on her' when she was in their bed. Ruby cannot roll over yet. Time of injury unclear; she noticed crying when she picked Ruby up at 6 am, but Ruby was 'unsettled' from about midnight when Kayla was at her night-fill job at the supermarket and Josh was looking after her. Presentation was delayed about 8 hours. The bruise on the cheek: 'she must have hit herself with a toy'.

Ruby's background: Born at 37 weeks, 2.8 kg, no NICU stay. Formula fed. Not yet rolling or sitting. Weight on the 25th centile (dropped from the 50th). Immunisations: missed the 4-month vaccines. No previous fractures, no known bone disease, no family history of brittle bones or bleeding disorders. One previous ED visit at 3 months for 'a bruise on her ear' that was not followed up.

Social: Kayla lives with Josh (24), not Ruby's biological father, in a rented unit. Josh is unemployed and 'gets stressed when she cries'. HIDDEN CUE 1 (only if asked privately about safety): Josh has shoved Kayla and smashed things when angry; he has shaken the cot 'to shut her up'. Kayla's family are in Cairns. HIDDEN CUE 2 (only if asked about her own mood): she feels 'flat and exhausted all the time', cries daily and sometimes wishes she could 'just disappear', but has no plan to harm herself or Ruby. Smokes, occasional cannabis.

Ideas: Hopes it is an accident. Concerns: That Child Safety will take Ruby away. Expectations: Wants Ruby's leg fixed and to go home.

If the doctor explains honestly that the injury needs investigation and reporting, and that everyone's focus is Ruby's safety, she cries but cooperates.

markingCriteria: Introduces self, acknowledges the mother's distress and maintains a calm, non-judgemental, non-accusatory approach throughout
Takes a detailed history of the injury: when, where, who was present, mechanism, and the timeline, noting inconsistencies and delay in presentation
Recognises that the mechanism is inconsistent with the injury and the child's developmental stage (non-mobile infant)
Asks about the bruise and previous injuries or presentations
Takes a birth, feeding, growth, developmental and immunisation history
Asks about family history of bone disease or bleeding disorders
Takes a social history: household members, carers, supports, family violence, substance use and parental mental health, including asking privately about safety
Screens the mother's mood and safety (postnatal depression, thoughts of self-harm or of harming the baby)
Explains honestly and without blame that this type of injury in a young baby must be investigated, that Ruby will be admitted, and that a report to Child Safety is required

Tells the examiner: suspected non-accidental injury; mandatory report to Queensland Child Safety; admission for protection; skeletal survey, CT head/ophthalmology consideration, FBC, coagulation, bone biochemistry; child protection team and social work involvement; document verbatim
Addresses the mother's welfare: referral for her own mental health and domestic violence support
expectedDiagnosis: Suspected non-accidental injury (physical abuse): spiral femoral fracture and facial bruising in a non-mobile infant with an inconsistent history; maternal depression and family violence
teachingPoints: 'Those who don't cruise rarely bruise': any bruise or fracture in a non-mobile infant is a red flag for physical abuse, and facial or ear bruising is particularly concerning (TEN-4-FACESp rule).
Red flags: inconsistent or changing history, mechanism not compatible with development, delayed presentation, previous unexplained injuries, faltering growth and missed immunisations.
Doctors are mandatory reporters in every Australian state and territory; the threshold is reasonable suspicion, not proof. In Queensland, report to Child Safety (and police if immediate danger).
Workup for suspected NAI in infants: skeletal survey, CT brain, ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhages, FBC, coagulation, calcium, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, PTH, and consider urine for toxicology.
Document the history verbatim with times, and do not interrogate: the doctor's role is to assess, protect and report, not investigate the crime.
Family violence and maternal mental illness frequently coexist with child abuse; support the parent as well as protecting the child.

title: Low mood in a 47-year-old farmer
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in a rural town in the Wheatbelt of Western Australia. Mr Craig Dawson, a 47-year-old farmer, has come in at his wife's insistence because he has been 'not himself' for a few months. He says he is only here for a script for sleeping tablets.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a focused history to assess his mental state and risk
- Tell Mr Dawson your assessment
- Outline an immediate management and safety plan with him
tasks: Take a history of depressive symptoms and a structured suicide risk assessment
Explain the assessment
Develop an immediate management and safety plan

patient.name: Craig Dawson
patient.persona: Quiet, flat, makes little eye contact, gives short answers. Uses stoic country phrases ('she'll be right', 'just a bit crook'). Initially insists he only needs sleeping tablets. Opens up gradually if the doctor is patient, uses open questions and shows genuine concern. Will only disclose suicidal thoughts and his access to firearms if asked directly and non-judgementally.
patient.openingLine: Look, I'm only here 'cause the wife made me. I just need something to help me sleep and I'll be right.
patient.script:
HPI: Four months of low mood since the third failed harvest in a row and the bank refusing to extend the farm loan. Wakes at 3 am most nights and cannot get back to sleep, worrying about money. Loss of interest in footy and fishing, which he used to love. Tired all the time, poor concentration, 'can't make decisions'. Appetite reduced, lost about 5 kg. Feels he has let his family and his late father down ('Dad ran this farm 40 years, I've stuffed it in five'). Irritable with his wife and kids. No psychotic symptoms, no manic episodes.

Risk: HIDDEN CUE 1 (only if asked directly about suicidal thoughts): Thinks most days that his family would be better off with the life insurance. Two weeks ago he sat in the shed with his rifle for an hour, then put it away because he thought of his daughter finding him. Has not told anyone. No previous attempts. Protective factors: his two children (14 and 11), his wife. HIDDEN CUE 2: Keeps two rifles and a shotgun for vermin in the gun safe in the shed; he has the key.

PMH: Back pain. Meds: none; occasional paracetamol. Allergies: nil.
Family: Father died by suicide 8 years ago during the last drought (only if asked about family history). Mother lives in town.

Social: Wheat and sheep farmer, farm has been in the family three generations, significant debt. Drinks 6-8 beers most nights 'to switch off', more than a year ago. Non-smoker. Married to Leanne; she is supportive but he has not told her about the loan. No other supports; 'blokes out here don't talk about this stuff'.

Ideas: Thinks he is 'just stressed and tired'. Concerns: Being seen as weak; losing his firearms licence if he tells a doctor. Expectations: Sleeping tablets.

Will agree to his wife holding the gun safe key, or to a mate or local police storing the firearms, if the doctor explains why with care. Agrees to come back tomorrow.

markingCriteria: Builds rapport with a stoic reluctant patient, acknowledges his reason for attending and uses open questions and empathy
Screens for core depressive symptoms (mood, anhedonia) and associated symptoms (sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, guilt, psychomotor change), with duration and functional impact
Identifies precipitating stressors: financial loss, drought, farm debt, sense of failure
Asks directly and sensitively about suicidal ideation, plans, intent, preparatory acts and previous attempts
Specifically asks about access to means, identifying the firearms
Elicits risk factors (family history of suicide, male, rural, alcohol, financial stress, isolation) and protective factors
Screens for alcohol use, psychotic features and bipolarity
Explains the assessment: moderate to severe major depressive episode with significant suicide risk, in a non-stigmatising way

Develops a collaborative safety plan: removal of firearms from the home with the patient's agreement, involving his wife with consent, crisis contacts (Lifeline 13 11 14, Suicide Call Back Service), and reducing alcohol

Avoids prescribing benzodiazepines or large quantities of potentially lethal medication; discusses treatment options (psychological therapy via a Mental Health Treatment Plan, antidepressant) and considers rural supports
Considers need for urgent specialist input (community mental health team, telepsychiatry) and knows the threshold for involuntary assessment
Arranges very close follow-up (within 24-48 hours) and documents the risk assessment
expectedDiagnosis: Major depressive episode (moderate to severe) with high suicide risk: active ideation, a recent rehearsal with a firearm and access to firearms
teachingPoints: Ask about suicide directly: asking does not increase risk. Explore ideation, plan, intent, rehearsal, access to means, and protective factors.
Rural men, farmers and people with a family history of suicide or financial stress are high-risk groups in Australia; firearms are a common method in rural suicides.

Means restriction saves lives: arrange for firearms to be removed or stored off site with agreement. Doctors in all states may notify police about a firearm holder who is a risk to themselves or others.
Do not prescribe sedatives in a patient with suicidal thoughts and heavy alcohol use; if an antidepressant is started, prescribe small quantities and review within 1-2 weeks.
A GP Mental Health Treatment Plan gives access to Medicare-rebated psychology (including telehealth); link to rural programs and crisis lines (Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue).
Document the risk assessment and the safety plan, and involve family with consent.

title: Strange behaviour in a 21-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are an HMO in the emergency department of a rural hospital in Lismore, NSW. Mr Ethan Brooks, a 21-year-old university student, has been brought in by his mother, who says he has been acting strangely for six weeks: he has stopped going to classes and has covered his bedroom windows with foil. He agreed to come in. His physical observations are normal and a urine drug screen is pending.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a brief history and perform a mental state examination
- Tell the examiner your findings, most likely diagnosis and differentials
- Outline your initial management
tasks: Take a brief history and perform a mental state examination
Present MSE findings, diagnosis and differentials
Outline initial management including risk assessment

patient.name: Ethan Brooks
patient.persona: Guarded and suspicious, speaks quietly, glances at the door and the ceiling. Answers some questions briefly, others with odd explanations. Believes the university and 'the government' are monitoring him through his laptop and phone. Hears voices commenting on him. Becomes more open if the doctor is calm, non-confrontational and does not argue with his beliefs. Will only reveal command hallucinations about his housemate if asked about what the voices say.
patient.openingLine: Is this room safe? Who else can hear this? My mum thinks I'm crazy but I know what's going on.
patient.script:
HPI: For about two months he believes lecturers and 'ASIO' are monitoring him through the webcam, phone and Wi-Fi; covered windows with foil to stop signals. Hears two male voices, outside his head, commenting on what he does ('he's going to the kitchen now') and calling him a loser. HIDDEN CUE 1 (only if asked what the voices say to him or whether they tell him to do things): In the last week one voice has told him his housemate is 'one of them' and that he 'needs to deal with him'. He has started keeping a kitchen knife under his pillow 'for protection'. He has not acted on it. Sleeping 3-4 hours a night, eating little, stopped showering regularly. Thinks his thoughts are being broadcast. Denies thoughts of suicide, but says 'sometimes it'd be easier not to be here' (passive).

No mood elevation, no grandiosity. No head injury, no seizures.

Substances: HIDDEN CUE 2: Smokes cannabis daily for three years, stronger 'hydro' for the past six months, about 2 grams a day. Occasional methamphetamine at parties (last used a month ago). Drinks on weekends.

PMH: Nil. Meds: nil. Allergies: nil.
Family history: Maternal uncle has schizophrenia.

Social: Second-year engineering student, lives in a share house with two housemates. Previously a good student. Stopped seeing friends. Not working. Drives an old car.

Insight: Poor; thinks he is not unwell but agrees he is 'stressed and not sleeping'. Will accept 'something to help me sleep'. Reluctant to stay in hospital but will agree if the doctor is respectful and explains.
patient.examFindings:
Mental state examination (the examiner will provide these observations if asked):
Appearance: Thin young man, dishevelled, unwashed hair, wearing a hoodie pulled up. Poor eye contact; repeatedly scans the room.
Behaviour: Guarded, suspicious, restless, sits near the door. Mild psychomotor agitation. Not aggressive.
Speech: Quiet, normal rate, some latency, occasionally vague.
Mood (subjective): 'Stressed'. Affect: Restricted, anxious, perplexed at times.
Thought form: Mild loosening of associations, some tangentiality.
Thought content: Persecutory delusions of surveillance by the university and government; thought broadcasting. Command hallucinations directed at the housemate (if elicited). Passive death wish, no active suicidal plan.
Perception: Auditory hallucinations: two male voices in the third person giving a running commentary, and second person derogatory and command content. Appears to respond to unseen stimuli at times.
Cognition: Alert, oriented to time, place and person. Attention mildly reduced.
Insight: Poor. Judgement: Impaired.
Physical: Observations normal; no signs of intoxication or withdrawal. Neurological screen normal.

markingCriteria: Introduces self, ensures safety of the environment for self and patient, and approaches in a calm non-confrontational manner
Takes a brief history of the psychotic symptoms, their duration and functional decline
Performs a structured MSE covering appearance, behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought form, thought content, perception, cognition, insight and judgement
Elicits delusions and hallucinations without colluding with or arguing against them
Specifically asks about command hallucinations and identifies the risk to the housemate and the knife
Assesses risk to self (including passive death wish), to others, and vulnerability
Takes a substance use history identifying heavy daily cannabis and methamphetamine use
Asks about family history of psychotic illness

Presents findings concisely and states first-episode psychosis (probable schizophreniform disorder), with differentials of substance-induced psychotic disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder with psychotic features, and organic causes
Outlines investigations to exclude organic causes: FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, calcium, glucose, B12, HIV and syphilis serology, urine drug screen, consider CT or MRI brain

Outlines management: mental health team review, admission (voluntary if possible, otherwise assessment under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007), low-dose second-generation antipsychotic, managing risk to the housemate (duty of care), early psychosis program referral
Addresses cannabis use and involves the family with consent
expectedDiagnosis: First-episode psychosis (probable schizophreniform disorder, differential cannabis or methamphetamine induced psychosis) with command hallucinations and risk to others
teachingPoints: Structure the MSE: Appearance, Behaviour, Speech, Mood/affect, Thought form, Thought content, Perception, Cognition, Insight, Judgement; present it in that order.
Always ask what the voices say and whether they tell you to do things; command hallucinations with a plan or weapon mean high risk to others.
Schizophreniform disorder is a psychotic illness of 1-6 months; schizophrenia requires 6 months or more (DSM-5-TR).
Exclude organic and substance causes: urine drug screen, bloods, and imaging if atypical features. Heavy daily high-potency cannabis roughly quadruples the risk of psychosis.
Early psychosis services (for example headspace early psychosis programs) improve outcomes; start a low-dose second-generation antipsychotic and monitor metabolic effects (RANZCP guidelines).
Each state has its own Mental Health Act: involuntary assessment requires mental illness and a need for care to prevent serious harm to self or others, when no less restrictive option is available.

title: Alcohol use in a 52-year-old man
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in a suburban clinic in Geelong. Mr Steve Mitchell, a 52-year-old sales manager, has come in for the results of blood tests arranged at an insurance medical. The results show GGT 186 U/L (normal under 60), ALT 72 U/L, AST 94 U/L, MCV 102 fL, and are otherwise normal. His BP today is 148/96 mmHg.

Your tasks are to:
- Explain the results and take a focused alcohol history
- Provide a brief intervention
- Outline a management plan
tasks: Explain the results and take a focused alcohol history
Provide a brief intervention using motivational techniques
Outline a management and follow-up plan

patient.name: Steve Mitchell
patient.persona: Confident, jovial, a bit defensive ('everyone in sales has a drink, Doc'). Minimises intake and jokes about it. Becomes more honest if the doctor is non-judgemental and uses a curious, respectful tone. Will only reveal morning drinking, drink-driving and his wife's ultimatum if asked directly and sensitively.
patient.openingLine: So, the insurance mob wanted bloods. All good? I feel fit as a fiddle.
patient.script:
Alcohol: Initially says 'a couple of beers after work'. On specific questioning: 4-5 schooners of full-strength beer at the pub after work on weekdays plus 2-3 glasses of wine with dinner; on weekends a bottle of wine plus beers at the footy. Estimated 60-80 standard drinks a week. Drinking at this level for about 8 years, increasing since his divorce 3 years ago and remarriage. HIDDEN CUE 1 (only if asked about morning drinking or withdrawal): Has started having 'a quick one' (vodka) in the morning to stop his hands shaking, and sweats at night if he does not drink. Once had a 'funny turn' when he stopped for three days, felt he saw insects on the wall. No known seizures.

CAGE: Has felt he should cut down, annoyed when his wife mentions it, feels guilty, and morning eye-opener (4/4).

HIDDEN CUE 2 (only if asked about driving or problems from drinking): Drives home from the pub most nights; nearly hit a cyclist two months ago. His wife Jenny has said she will leave if he does not 'sort it out'.

PMH: Hypertension, not on treatment. Reflux. Gout attack last year.
Meds: Pantoprazole 40 mg daily. Allergies: nil.
Family: Father was 'a big drinker', died of liver cancer at 64.

Social: Sales manager for a car dealership, entertains clients. Smoked, quit 10 years ago. No other drugs. Lives with wife Jenny and her teenage son.

Ideas: Thinks his drinking is normal for his job. Concerns: That his liver is 'shot' like his dad's; losing his licence or job. Expectations: Wants to hear the tests are fine.

Readiness: Contemplative. If the doctor links his father's illness, the blood results and his wife's concern in a non-confrontational way, he admits 'yeah, maybe it's got out of hand' and is willing to try cutting down with support.

markingCriteria: Establishes rapport, checks his understanding and explains the abnormal results in plain language (pattern consistent with alcohol-related liver injury and macrocytosis)
Takes a quantified alcohol history in standard drinks, including type, amount, pattern and duration
Uses a validated screening tool (AUDIT or AUDIT-C, CAGE) and recognises alcohol dependence
Screens for withdrawal features including morning drinking, tremor, and previous complicated withdrawal (hallucinations, seizures)
Asks about consequences: driving, relationships, work, legal and physical health
Explores mental health, other substances and family history
Delivers a brief intervention using FRAMES or motivational interviewing: feedback, responsibility, advice, menu of options, empathy, self-efficacy
Advises that the NHMRC 2020 guideline is no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day
Advises that he must not drink and drive, addresses the risk to others, and considers fitness-to-drive implications

Recognises that he should not stop suddenly without support and plans supervised withdrawal (home or inpatient depending on risk) with thiamine, and considers relapse prevention medication (acamprosate, naltrexone)
Plans further workup: repeat LFTs, liver ultrasound, fibrosis assessment (FIB-4 or elastography), hepatitis serology, and management of BP
Offers supports (DirectLine, counselling, AA or SMART Recovery) and arranges follow-up
expectedDiagnosis: Alcohol use disorder (dependence) with alcohol-related liver injury and macrocytosis, previous complicated withdrawal, and drink-driving
teachingPoints: NHMRC 2020 Australian guidelines: to reduce health risks, healthy adults should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 standard drinks on any one day. One standard drink is 10 g of alcohol.
Always quantify in standard drinks; a schooner of full-strength beer is about 1.6 standard drinks and a restaurant glass of wine about 1.5.
Brief interventions (FRAMES) in general practice reduce harmful drinking; match the approach to the stage of change.
Dependent drinkers with previous withdrawal hallucinations or seizures need planned, medically supervised withdrawal; give thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Relapse prevention: acamprosate or naltrexone are PBS-listed; disulfiram is less commonly used.
Isolated raised GGT with AST greater than ALT and macrocytosis is a typical alcohol pattern; assess fibrosis and screen for other liver disease.

title: Open disclosure of a medication error
candidateBrief:
You are an intern on the surgical ward of a metropolitan hospital in Sydney. Mrs Margaret Hughes, a 71-year-old woman, is day 2 after an elective total knee replacement. Last night she was given an intravenous dose of cefazolin despite a documented allergy to penicillin (urticarial rash). She developed an itchy rash on her chest and arms within 30 minutes, which settled with oral antihistamine. Her observations remained stable throughout. The error has been reported via the incident management system and your consultant has asked you to speak with her.

Your tasks are to:
- Explain to Mrs Hughes what has happened
- Respond to her questions and concerns
- Outline what will happen next
tasks: Explain the incident honestly using open disclosure principles
Respond to her concerns and questions
Outline the next steps and follow-up

patient.name: Margaret Hughes
patient.persona: Retired schoolteacher, articulate and initially polite, becomes angry when she realises it was an error ('I told three different people I was allergic!'). Wants honesty and an apology. Calms if the doctor listens, apologises sincerely and avoids jargon or blame. Only mentions her fear that this could happen again with her husband, who has dementia and is also in hospital, if asked what is worrying her most.
patient.openingLine: Doctor, the nurse said you wanted to talk to me about last night. Was it the new antibiotic that gave me that rash?
patient.script:
What she knows: She had an itchy red rash last night after 'a drip' and was given a tablet. The nurse this morning looked uncomfortable and said a doctor would come and explain.

Allergy history: She had hives after amoxicillin in 1998 and has told the pre-admission clinic, the anaesthetist and the ward nurse. She has a red allergy wristband on.

Current state: Rash has almost gone, some mild itch remaining. No breathing difficulty, no lip or tongue swelling. Knee is sore but she is mobilising with the physio. Otherwise feels well.

PMH: Osteoarthritis, hypertension, hypothyroidism. Meds: amlodipine 5 mg, levothyroxine 100 mcg, paracetamol, enoxaparin (post-op), oxycodone as needed. Allergy: penicillin (urticaria).

Social: Married to Ron, 78, who has Alzheimer's dementia and is currently in respite care. HIDDEN CUE 1: Ron has a severe allergy to aspirin; she is very worried that if this can happen to her, who is articulate, it could happen to Ron who cannot speak up for himself. Two adult children, daughter Sue is a nurse.

Ideas: Suspects a mistake. Concerns: Whether she is safe now, whether she will have long-term effects, whether it will happen again, and her husband. HIDDEN CUE 2: She asks, 'Who did this? I want to make a complaint', and wants to know if the nurse will be punished.

Expectations: A sincere apology, an honest explanation, to know what is being done to prevent it happening again, and how to make a complaint.

If the doctor apologises clearly, explains without blaming individuals, and explains review and prevention, she accepts. If the doctor is defensive, vague or blames a colleague, she becomes more upset.

markingCriteria: Prepares appropriately: private setting, offers to have a support person present, introduces self and role
Checks what she already knows and what she would like to know
Gives a clear, honest factual explanation that she was given an antibiotic that she should not have received because of her penicillin allergy
Offers a sincere apology ('I am sorry') early, without speculation or blaming individuals
Allows her to express anger and responds with empathy and active listening
Explains the clinical impact: a mild allergic reaction that has settled; checks for any ongoing symptoms and explains monitoring
Explains what is being done: incident reported, review underway, allergy documentation checked, and learnings will be shared with her
Addresses her concern about her husband and offers to ensure his allergy is flagged and communicated
Explains her right to make a complaint and how (patient liaison, Health Care Complaints Commission in NSW) without being defensive
Does not identify or blame the individual staff member, and explains the systems approach to review
Arranges follow-up: senior or consultant meeting, written summary, and updates on the outcome of the review
Documents the disclosure conversation in the medical record
expectedDiagnosis: Adverse drug reaction (mild urticarial reaction) due to administration of a cephalosporin despite documented penicillin allergy; medication error requiring open disclosure
teachingPoints: The Australian Open Disclosure Framework (ACSQHC) requires an open discussion with the patient and family after any incident causing harm: apologise, explain the facts, the consequences, and the steps taken to manage it and prevent recurrence.
Saying 'I am sorry' is not an admission of liability; apology laws in all Australian states protect an apology from being used as an admission.
Avoid speculation and blame: the incident will be reviewed through the hospital's clinical governance process (for example a root cause analysis), and findings are shared with the patient.

Low-risk penicillin allergy histories are now often delabelled, but a documented allergy must never be overridden without specialist assessment; cefazolin has a dissimilar side chain and cross-reactivity is low, but the process failure still requires disclosure.
Patients have the right to complain: internally via the patient liaison or consumer service, and externally to the state health complaints body (HCCC in NSW).
Document the disclosure conversation, who was present and what was agreed.

title: A 15-year-old requesting contraception
candidateBrief:
You are a general practitioner in a suburban clinic in Brisbane. Zoe Clarke, a 15-year-old girl, has come in on her own after school. She has seen you before with her mother for asthma. She tells the receptionist she wants to talk about 'something private'.

Your tasks are to:
- Take a relevant history from Zoe
- Assess her capacity to consent and address confidentiality
- Discuss contraception options and a management plan
tasks: Take a psychosocial and sexual health history (HEEADSSS)
Assess her capacity to consent (mature minor) and explain confidentiality and its limits
Discuss contraception options and a management plan

patient.name: Zoe Clarke
patient.persona: Nervous, embarrassed, avoids eye contact at first, speaks quietly. Worried the doctor will tell her mum. Becomes more relaxed and open once confidentiality is explained. Articulate and thoughtful once comfortable. Only reveals the recent unprotected sex if asked about the last time she had sex or whether condoms were used every time.
patient.openingLine: Um, hi. This is kind of awkward. Can you promise you won't tell my mum?
patient.script:
Reason: Wants to go on the pill. Has had a boyfriend, Josh, for five months. He is 16 and in Year 11 at her school. They have had sex about four times over the past month, consensual, 'both of us wanted to', no pressure, no gifts or money, no drugs or alcohol involved. First sexual partner for both.

HIDDEN CUE 1 (only if asked when they last had sex and whether a condom was used): Two days ago (about 50 hours ago) the condom broke. LMP 12 days ago, regular 28-day cycles. She has not done anything about it yet.

Gynae: Menarche at 12. Periods regular, a bit heavy with cramps. No discharge, no pain with sex, no bleeding after sex. Never had an STI test.

PMH: Mild asthma. Meds: Salbutamol as needed. Allergies: nil. No migraine with aura, no history of blood clots, non-smoker, BP normal at last visit.

Family history: No clotting disorders known, otherwise nil significant.

HEEADSSS: Home: lives with mum and stepdad; gets on okay with mum, 'she'd freak out though'. Education: Year 10, doing well, wants to study nursing. Eating: normal. Activities: netball, friends. Drugs: tried alcohol at a party once; no smoking or vaping; no other drugs. Sexuality: as above, attracted to boys. Safety: feels safe at home and in the relationship; seatbelts; no online risk. HIDDEN CUE 2 (only if asked about mood): Has been feeling a bit anxious about exams and about 'getting caught', but no low mood, self-harm or suicidal thoughts.

Ideas: Wants the pill. Concerns: That her mum finds out, including through Medicare statements. Expectations: A script today.

She understands risks and benefits well when explained, can weigh information and repeat it back. She is open to considering an implant or IUD if explained, and agrees to an STI test.

markingCriteria: Welcomes her, sees her alone, and explains confidentiality and its limits early (risk of serious harm to self or others, or abuse)
Takes a HEEADSSS psychosocial history
Takes a sexual history including partner age, consent, coercion, number of partners and contraceptive use
Assesses the relationship for legality and safety: age of partner, power imbalance, coercion, and recognises this as similar-age consensual activity not requiring a child safety report
Assesses capacity to consent as a mature minor (Gillick competence): understands, retains, weighs and communicates the decision
Identifies the condom failure 2 days ago and offers emergency contraception (levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72 hours, or ulipristal within 120 hours; copper IUD most effective)
Takes a medical history for contraindications to oestrogen (MEC): migraine with aura, VTE, smoking, BP
Discusses contraceptive options, emphasising LARCs (implant, hormonal IUD) as most effective, as well as the combined pill, and dual protection with condoms
Offers STI screening (chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT on self-collected swab or urine) and discusses HPV vaccination status
Addresses Medicare confidentiality (own Medicare card from age 15, adolescent privacy options) and encourages, but does not insist on, involving a trusted adult
Arranges a pregnancy test in 3-4 weeks and follow-up, and safety-nets
expectedDiagnosis: Contraception request in a mature minor with recent unprotected intercourse requiring emergency contraception
teachingPoints: Adolescents aged under 16 can consent to their own treatment if they are a mature minor (Gillick competent); document the assessment. In Australia, young people can have their own Medicare card from age 15.

The age of consent is 16 in most states and territories (17 in SA and Tasmania); similar-age consensual activity generally has legal defences, but coercion, a large age gap, or a partner in a position of authority should prompt a child safety assessment and mandatory report.

Always ask about recent unprotected sex: emergency contraception options are levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (within 72 hours, less effective later), ulipristal 30 mg (within 120 hours) or a copper IUD (within 120 hours, most effective).
LARCs (etonogestrel implant, levonorgestrel IUD) are first-line for young people; use quick-start with a pregnancy test in 3-4 weeks.
HEEADSSS gives structure to the adolescent psychosocial history; confidentiality should be explained at the start, including its limits.
Offer opportunistic chlamydia testing to all sexually active young people under 30 (RACGP Red Book, ASHM guidance).
